# Tips from past games

Written 2026-10-11 10:01 by opus-5.5 with `uv run tips.py build`, from the 262 active entries of tips_notebook.json (50 games). Players never see this preamble; they see every section below. Earlier sheets are in history/.

## Everyone
- Ballots are secret, so keep a notepad of every nomination and trial: each player's stated vote, the announced totals and your own. Vote as you said you would and explain any switch first; a mismatch with the totals is a lead, never a hang on its own. (seen in 30 games)
- Totals can be manipulated. A trial total above the voter count means a Ballot Stuffer, and a Fixer silently flips one player's trial votes. Yes/No nomination counts can't be altered, so they are the cleanest liar check. (seen in 2 games)
- A visit shows a destination, not an action. But a corroborated Lookout or Tracker naming X as the only unexplained visitor to a Katana victim is near-proof; don't let 'a visit isn't an attack' acquit X. (seen in 32 games)
- Before voting Guilty, name one concrete mechanical fit: an unexplained Evil read on a Vanilla claim, a broken visit claim, or a group result where elimination leaves one name. A role-block fully explains a missing result, so that is never a contradiction. (seen in 36 games)
- Each night write your planned target in your will, and post results publicly by day. The result of the night you die never reaches your will. (seen in 29 games)
- Answer a direct question about your night action in one plain sentence the first time it is asked; days of evasion become a case of their own. (seen in 9 games)
- Tokens die with you. Spend one-shot tokens on the first Day or night they can change a vote or remove a threat, and spend a puppet or doubled ballot at least a night before a likely death. (seen in 4 games)

## Village
- Post your role, target and exact result in your first speech after getting it, and counterclaim any copier at once with your full log. Results held back look retrofitted. (seen in 18 games)
- Never announce tonight's target, in public or by PM. A Wiretap may read every PM, and a named target tells blockers and the Katana where to go. (seen in 24 games)
- On Day 2, power roles with no result should not hint at their role or lead loudly. The most organized voice is the usual Night 2 kill. (seen in 24 games)
- Once someone is shown Yakuza mechanically, look at who defended them or pushed to delay their hang. Treat PM links as leads only, since Jesters and Executioners leave trails on purpose. (seen in 30 games)
- Before any hang, ask whether the nominee wins by being hanged. If you must hang a likely Jester, use a bare Guilty majority and keep confirmed power roles on Innocent. (seen in 16 games)
- Hunt Neutral killers deliberately. Read every cause of death, list unwatched Vanilla or unclaimed players and survivors with no protector, and hang the best suspect before the final two, when you can no longer hang them. (seen in 2 games)
- Surviving an attack proves nothing, since Arsonists and Serial Killers have Standard Defense. Ask the survivor at once who protected them. (seen in 17 games)

## Yakuza
- Don't defend a doomed teammate. If your team's votes can't stop the hang, vote Guilty with the town, because hidden Innocent votes show in the totals. (seen in 38 games)
- Send no daytime PMs about team plans, and none to teammates on Day 2; plan in night chat. (seen in 34 games)
- Fake-claim a Village role whose tokens and real visits match yours. Never claim or name a Yakuza-only role, and never switch claims once cornered. (seen in 19 games)
- Every member must submit the agreed Katana holder and target every night; one missing vote can cancel the kill. (seen in 20 games)
- Never flatly deny a visit that an FT count, map group or Lookout could expose. Agree a cover in night chat, and move the Katana off any holder a watcher has named. (seen in 22 games)
- After a failed Katana attack, kill or block the likely protector instead of retrying blindly. Prioritize running counts (Fortune Teller, Census Taker) and Party Animals with block logs. (seen in 21 games)
- Use Clerk rigs, puppets and cleans early, but never rig a Day when a teammate is the likely nominee. (seen in 20 games)

## Neutral
- If innate Defense saves you, deny being attacked. If you must explain it, pick one claim at once and never switch. (seen in 6 games)

## Sheriff
- The Katana holder reads Not Evil, so say so whenever you post a Not Evil result. A lone last Yakuza reads Not Evil every night. (seen in 19 games)

## Coroner
- Examine bodies that settle live questions: one side of a duplicate claim, or a hanged suspect. Post the night, target and role in one message the next Day, and skip cleaned bodies. (seen in 3 games)

## Medic
- Use free Standard protection on likely Katana targets, vary your pattern, and never announce targets. Spend a token on self-protection within a night or two of claiming, and never claim you 'saw' a save. (seen in 24 games)

## Vigilante
- Set a trigger by Day 2-3 and fire a Basic shot on a real lead rather than dying with all tokens. A Basic shot that fails without a credible Medic points to innate Defense, so post it. (seen in 11 games)

## Smuggler
- A swap moves only actions aimed at the two swapped players. Aim the Katana at a decoy and swap the decoy with the protected real target, or swap yourself with a Villager to dodge a check. Plan it in night chat rather than vetoing it. (seen in 2 games)

## Arsonist
- Ignite once 3 living players are doused, or 2 if you are being questioned. Have a claim ready that explains your douse visits. (seen in 12 games)

rules:
=== PART 1: THE GAME ===

R1 (Overview and winning)
You are playing a Mafia-style game with around 10 players (depending on setup), each in a faction. An omniscient
moderator runs the game. The game alternates Night and Day phases, starting with Night 1: there is no Day 1, so
the first Day is Day 2 (players write their first will before Night 1).
- For most roles, you win iff your faction wins. A faction typically wins iff it has players alive at the end.
- The game ends as soon as all living players, ignoring roles that never block wins, belong to one faction. This is
  checked after every death; deaths that happen together at night are checked together.
- Some Neutral roles never block another faction's win (their role says so); their own wins don't depend on how
  the game ends.

R2 (Factions)
- Village (Good): the largest faction, but with weaker roles and less information.
- Yakuza (Evil): fewer players, stronger roles; they know each other and share a night chat.
- Neutral: each Neutral player is their own one-person faction, even if two players have the same Neutral role.
The list of roles in the game is not public. A role may appear more than once in a game, except these unique
roles, which appear at most once: Smuggler, Vulture.

R15 (Alignments)
Every player has one of three alignments: Good (Village), Evil (Yakuza) or Neutral. Some roles and effects change
how a player's alignment appears; see R19.

R18 (Terms)
- Living players: players who haven't died or left. Every count in these rules ("majority", "random player")
  means living players unless it says otherwise.
- Majority: strictly more than half; exactly half is not a majority.
- Action: anything a role does at night by choice or by its rules (investigating, shooting, blocking, ...).
- Visit: an action on another player counts as A visiting B, unless it is an Astral Visit (R6).
- Astral Visit: an action that is not a visit. Abilities that react to visits (Tracker, Lookout, Trapper,
  Fortune Teller) never see or react to it.
- Alignment check: a result that reports alignment (Sheriff, Seer). See R19 for what they see.
- Exact-role check: a result that reports or tests an exact role (Oracle, Diviner, Ritualist, Mortician, Coroner,
  Talent Agent, a Vigilante's kill).
- Token: a limited-use resource a role starts with. Spent tokens are gone; a role-blocked action spends none.

R11 (The circle)
Players sit in a circle. The dead (and players who leave) are removed from it.

=== PART 2: THE DAY ===

R4 (Day phase, chat, nominations and trials)
Chat:
- There is a public chat and private chats between exactly two players.
- Private messages are not secret: whenever A sends B a private message, everyone sees that A sent B a private
  message, but only A and B see its contents.
Nominations:
- Any player may publicly nominate someone, including themself. All chat stops at once.
- Everyone votes Yes/No at the same time; nobody sees another vote before casting their own. The nominator votes
  Yes by default. There are no abstentions: a player who doesn't vote counts as voting No. Votes are secret: once
  all votes are in, only the number of Yes votes is announced (the nominator is named), never who voted which way.
  Each voter is privately reminded of their own vote.
- If a majority of all votes counted are Yes, the nominee goes on trial.
Trials:
- The nominee says the first public message and may defend themself; others may chat publicly and privately.
  After everyone else has had a turn, the nominee gets one last public message before the vote.
- Then everyone votes Guilty/Innocent at the same time (no abstentions: a player who doesn't vote counts as voting
  Innocent). Votes are secret: only the Guilty and Innocent totals are announced, never who voted which way. Each
  voter is privately reminded of their own vote.
- If a majority of all votes counted are Guilty, the nominee is Executed by Hanging, a Divine Attack, and the Day
  ends immediately.
- If three nominations pass (failed ones don't count) and all three trials end Innocent, the Day ends.
- Some roles can change how votes are counted. If an announced vote total doesn't match the number of voters,
  a role manipulated the count on purpose; it is not an error. One use of such a role can change every trial
  that Day, so the number of changed totals doesn't show how many times a role was used.
Voting Yes or Guilty on yourself is allowed.

R16 (Day length)
Day chat goes around the circle in turns. Each Day the program picks a random living player to speak first;
turns then go around the circle from them in the same order every round. Besides the endings in R4, the Day ends when a full round passes in
which nobody sends a public message or nominates, except that anyone sent a private message during that round
first gets one last turn. The Day also ends after at most 8 rounds.

R22 (Speaking budget)
Day messages and nominations cost speaking budget. Each player earns budget every round of a Day, up to a cap,
and part of what they have left carries into the next Day. A message's price grows with its length and, after
the first rounds of a Day, with the round; private messages cost less than public ones. A nomination costs
budget too. On a trial turn prices are lower and each speaker also gets a trial-only budget, spent first and lost
when the turn ends; the accused's first defense message is free up to a set length. The program sets the
numbers for each game and tells every player at the start.

R23 (Swaps)
Some roles can swap two players for a night. Every action that night aimed at one of them (including the Katana's
attack and automatic actions such as the Ex-Con's visit or the Seer's pair) lands on the other instead, as if its
user had chosen that player. Only the swap itself is not moved (the swapping player's Katana vote is). Results name the player the action's
user chose, so a swapped action's result doesn't show the swap: a Sheriff who checked A learns B's alignment as
A's. A result that lists several players (e.g. a group around the target) is built around B, but A and B trade
places in the list, each named where the other would be; the roles, alignments and counts in it are still the real
players', so the rest of the group can still hint at the swap. A Lookout who watched A watches B instead, and a Tracker sees the player its target's action landed on.

R13 (Last wills)
Players may write and update a last will before Night 1, at the beginning of each Day (except those who died the
night before) and during any of their own Day turns. When a player dies, their last will is shared publicly at once.

=== PART 3: THE NIGHT ===

R5 (Night phase)
Chat is off for most players; some (usually a faction, like the Yakuza) have a private night chat. The moderator
wakes players one by one, or faction by faction, to act. When the Night ends, the moderator works out every
effect. By default, effects are announced publicly at the start of the next Day; some are not announced.

R7 (Optional actions)
Every ability is optional ("may") unless its role says "must": any player may choose not to act at Night, not to
use a Day ability, and not to spend a token. Effects a role has automatically, with no choice (e.g. the
Ex-Con's nightly visit), aren't optional, but a role-block still stops them (R9).

R6 (Visits)
- When A performs an action on B, A visits B, unless the action is an Astral Visit.
- A role that targets a player may target itself unless its text says otherwise (e.g. "other than yourself").
- A player whose role can target others but who targets themself shows as visiting themself.
- A player whose action can only affect themself does not show as visiting anyone.
- An action that targets no player (e.g. the Clerk's rig) is not a visit.
- A player who visits the same target with several actions in one night is one visitor to that target: anything
  that lists, counts or reacts to visitors (a watch, a Veteran's alert, a trap) treats them once.

R9 (Role-blocks)
A role-blocked player's actions that night have no effect, exactly as if they had chosen not to act: no visit,
no tokens spent. It lasts only that one night (not the next Day or later nights). Role-blocked players are told
they were role-blocked. Any player can be role-blocked unless their role says otherwise; blocking a player who
has no night action, or who chose not to act, has no other effect, but they are still told. A role-blocker learns
only whether the block failed because its target can't be role-blocked.

R10 (Simultaneous night resolution)
All night actions happen at the same time. Think of it as two steps: first everyone attempts their actions,
then all results happen together. So investigations that give their result at the end of the night (e.g. the
Seer's random pair) draw from and report on everyone alive when the night began, including players who die that
night.

R21 (Effects that outlast their user)
An effect set up at night for the following Day (e.g. a Clerk's rig, a Prosecutor's prosecution) still happens if
its user dies that night, unless it needs its user to act during that Day (e.g. a Puppeteer writing the puppet's
messages, a Ballot Stuffer's doubled vote); those lapse. Any token spent on it is gone either way (R18).

R20 (Night resolution checklist): a summary of the rules above, in the order the moderator applies them.
1. Remove actions of role-blocked players (R9), automatic ones included (the Ex-Con's visit, the Seer's pair).
   Party Animal, Pharmacist, Smuggler and Veteran can't be role-blocked. Swaps (R23) apply before anything else.
2. Work out who visits whom (R6), including the Katana holder's visit (R8) and the Ex-Con's random visit.
3. Attacks: each kills iff its level beats the target's Defense (R3). Defenses don't stack; the highest counts.
   Traps hit non-Village visitors (Trapper).
4. Results for investigators, using the visits and appearances (R19).
5. Notifications: attackers learn whether they succeeded, attacked players learn the attacking role (R3, with the
   Katana exception in R8), protectors learn nothing (R17), role-blocked players are told (R9), Yakuza learn each
   other's actions (R8).
6. Deaths are revealed at the start of the Day (R12); the win check runs on all of the night's deaths together (R1).

=== PART 4: ATTACKS, DEATH AND INFORMATION ===

R3 (Attack and Defense)
- Levels, lowest to highest: None, Basic, Standard, Strong, Divine. Players have Defense None by default.
- An Attack kills iff its level is strictly higher than the target's Defense.
- Defenses don't stack: a player with several sources of Defense has the highest of them.
- By default the attacker learns whether the Attack succeeded (not the target's Defense), and the target learns
  the role that attacked them (not the attacker's name or Attack level). The Katana is an exception (R8).

R17 (Protection feedback)
Protectors (e.g. the Medic) are never told whether their protection stopped an attack, and a protected player is
never told who protected them. A player who is attacked is still told as in R3.

R12 (Death reveals)
When someone dies, their cause of death (e.g. Katana, Vigilante, Execution by Hanging) and last will are revealed
publicly; their role and alignment are not. If several attacks were each fatal, every fatal cause is revealed;
attacks the player survived aren't. The dead leave the circle and can't take part in the game any more. A player
whose win ends their part in the game (a hanged Jester, an Executioner who leaves) is the exception: the
announcement of their win names their role.

R14 (Stall rule)
If a Day begins and nobody has died in the three previous Nights and three previous Days, everyone loses. Deaths
from last Night count even though they're announced today. Every death counts; leaving (like the Executioner's)
doesn't.

R19 (What investigations see)
Alignment checks (Sheriff: Evil / Not Evil; Seer: compares Good / Neutral / Evil) see a player's true alignment,
except:
- Yakuza holding the Katana at the end of the night: Good (Sheriff: Not Evil), even if they died that night.
- Player framed by the Fabricator that night: Evil.
- Ex-Con: Evil.
- Sheriff on Neutrals: Jester and Executioner read Evil; Serial Killer and Arsonist read Not Evil. (Seers see
  every Neutral as Neutral.)
The Census Taker's count is not an alignment check: it always sees true alignment, so none of the exceptions
above apply to it.
Exact-role checks see the true role. The Roleplayer is seen as "Roleplayer".
Token counts (Accountant) see the true total at the end of the night. The Roleplayer is seen as having 0 tokens,
even though they believe they have their fake role's tokens.
Visit-based results (Tracker, Lookout, Fortune Teller, Cartographer, Scout) are never changed by any of these.

=== PART 5: THE YAKUZA ===

R8 (Yakuza and the Katana)
- One random Yakuza starts with the Katana. The Yakuza share a private chat at night.
- Each night the Yakuza vote, at the same time, on who holds the Katana that night (and the next Day) and whom it
  attacks, if anyone. Both choices need a majority of living Yakuza; with two Yakuza alive, both must agree.
  Without a majority on a target, no attack happens; without a majority on a holder, the Katana doesn't move.
  A majority may move the Katana without attacking.
- The Katana attack is Standard and is dealt by whoever holds it at the end of the night. It is an action and a
  visit by that player (the new holder, if it moved that night): role-blocking them stops it, and Trackers see
  them visit the target. Moving or passing the Katana isn't an action: a role-block doesn't stop it (a blocked
  new holder still gets the Katana, but their attack fails), and it isn't a visit.
- The holder may also use their own role's night action.
- The holder appears Good to alignment checks that night (R19).
- The attacked player only learns they were attacked with the Katana, not the Yakuza role.
- At the end of the night, each Yakuza learns what actions the other Yakuza chose, but not their results
  (e.g. whether the Pharmacist's block worked) or whether a teammate was role-blocked.
- Role-blocked Yakuza still vote on the Katana's holder and target; the votes aren't actions.
- If the holder dies, the Katana passes to a random living Yakuza, if any; a holder who dies at night passes it on
  after that night's results. The living Yakuza are told who holds it now (and so learn that the holder died).

=== PART 6: ROLES ===

Every role lists the same fields. Defaults, unless a role says otherwise: Defense None, no tokens, appears as its
true alignment (R19), night action is a visit.

--- Village (Good) ---

Townsfolk (most villagers, helpful to the Village)

Vanilla Villager
  Night: none.

Investigative

Sheriff
  Night: may investigate one player. Learn Evil or Not Evil (alignment check, R19).

Tracker
  Night: may track one player. Learn whom they visited.

Lookout
  Night: may watch one player. Learn who visited them, not counting your own visit.

Seer
  Tokens: 1 seer token.
  Night: at the end of every night, you are told two random players other than yourself who were alive when the
  night began (players who die that night count, R10), and whether their alignments (Good/Neutral/Evil) are the
  same (alignment check, R19). Instead, you may spend a token to choose the
  two living players yourself (not including yourself). A chosen pair is a visit to both players; the random
  pair isn't a visit. A role-block stops both.

Fortune Teller
  Night: at the end of every night, you learn two numbers about that night, each labeled: how many players were
  visited (a player visited several times counts once), and how many players visited anyone (a player who visited
  several players counts once). This needs no action. Self-visits (R6) count in both numbers.
  Example: A holds the Katana, attacks B and also uses their own role's action on C, D visits B, and E protects
  themself. Visited: B, C and E, so 3. Visitors: A, D and E, so 3. Equal numbers don't mean nobody was visited
  twice.

Oracle
  Night: may guess one player's exact role (Astral Visit). At the end of the night, learn whether you were right.

Eavesdropper
  Night: may eavesdrop on one player. Only during the following Day (not the Night you eavesdrop), you read the contents of every private
  message they send or receive, as it is sent. Puppeted messages reach you as the puppet's (you aren't told about
  the puppeting). They aren't told.

Archivist
  Tokens: 1 archive token.
  Night: may spend the token to consult the archive. At the end of the night, let N be the number of players other
  than you who were alive when the night began (players who died that night count): you are shown N roles, in
  random order and without names, of which floor(0.5 * N) are real and the rest are fake. The real ones are the
  roles of floor(0.5 * N) of those players, chosen at random; a role appears as many times as it was drawn, so
  two drawn Vanilla Villagers show twice. This is an exact-role check (R19).
  Each fake is drawn at random from all the roles in these rules, including roles that are in the game, except
  that the result never shows a unique role (R2) twice.

Surveyor
  Tokens: 3 survey tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to survey one player other than yourself. The group is that player plus their nearest
  neighbor on each side in the circle (R11) among the players alive at the start of the night, skipping yourself
  and never counting anyone twice (so with only one or two other players alive, the group is smaller). You are
  told who was in the group and the exact role of one of them chosen at random, but not whose it is. Players who
  die that night can still be chosen. This is an exact-role check (R19).

Census Taker
  Night: may take a census around one player other than yourself (a visit to that player only).
  The program adds two other players drawn at random from everyone alive at the start of the night except you
  (players who die that night can be drawn; if fewer than two others are left, the group is smaller). It also
  draws at random whether to count Good or Evil players. You are told who was in the group, which alignment was
  counted, and how many of the group are of it. It counts true alignment and is not an alignment check (R19):
  the Katana holder, framed players and the Ex-Con count as what they really are, and
  Outsiders (e.g. the Roleplayer and the Ex-Con) count as Good. Neutral players are never
  counted, as either Good or Evil.

Coroner
  Tokens: 3 coroner tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to examine one player who died before the night began (not one who left the game, and not
  one who dies tonight). You learn their role, unless a Mortician cleaned them: then you learn only that. This is an
  Astral Visit (R6) and an exact-role check (R19).

Chronicler
  Tokens: 2 chronicler tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to mark one player other than yourself. This is a visit. The marked player isn't told.
  The mark lasts for the rest of the game, even after you die. If a marked player dies, at any time and of any
  cause, the announcement of their death also reveals their true role to everyone (an exact-role check, R19), and
  says they had been marked by a Chronicler (not by whom). A Mortician's clean beats the mark: a marked player who
  is cleaned has their role and will hidden, and the announcement says they had been marked but the clean hid their
  role. You can't mark a player you already marked. Marking a player another Chronicler already marked spends your
  token but adds nothing.

Auditor
  Night: may audit one player other than yourself. You learn every vote they cast during the Day just before this
  Night, in order: Yes or No on each nomination and Guilty or Innocent in each trial. If they cast none, you learn
  that. A doubled vote (Ballot Stuffer) shows as a single Guilty or Innocent.

Juror
  Night: may name two different players other than yourself (dead players allowed; Astral Visit). You learn how many
  times they voted the same way, over every Day so far, counted separately for trial votes (Guilty/Innocent) and
  nomination votes (Yes/No), e.g. "the same way in 3 of 4 trial votes and 5 of 9 nomination votes". Only votes
  both of them cast count, and not votes on the nomination or trial of either of them. A doubled vote (Ballot
  Stuffer) counts once. You learn only the totals, not which votes they agreed on.

Bloodhound
  Tokens: 2 scent tokens.
  Night: at the end of every night, code draws three random players other than you from those alive at the start of
  the night, and you learn their names and how many Attacks (R3) they have made in total this game, tonight's
  included, whether or not the Attacks killed anyone. Each player's Katana attacks, shots, alert or trap hits and
  so on all count; a role-blocked attack never happened, so it doesn't. This needs no action and a role-block
  doesn't stop it.
  Night: may also spend a token to track one player other than yourself: they take one of the three places that
  night and code draws the other two. A role-block stops the tracking (R9) but not the result.

Scrutineer
  Night: may scrutinize one player other than yourself who voted in the Day's trials (Astral Visit). Code adds two
  random other players who voted in those trials (never you), and you learn the three names and, for each trial of
  the Day just before this Night, how many of the three voted Guilty, e.g. "2 in the trial of Erin; 0 in the trial
  of Frank". You don't learn which of them voted which way. A doubled vote (Ballot Stuffer) counts once. If there
  was no trial that Day, you learn that.

Profiler
  Tokens: 3 profile tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to profile one player other than yourself. You learn three different roles, exactly one
  of which is that player's true role. Of the other two, one is drawn at random from the roles of the other players
  alive at the start of the night (including players who die that night, but not yourself), and the other from the
  roles that no player in the game has. At least one of the three is a Good role and at least one is not Good (Evil
  or Neutral), so a result never settles the player's alignment on its own; which of the two supplies the missing
  side is random. When no role fits a draw, that one is drawn from all roles in these rules instead. The three are
  different and listed in alphabetical order. This is an exact-role check (R19).

Cartographer
  Tokens: 2 map tokens.
  Night: at the end of every night, you learn the sizes of that night's visit groups. Link two players whenever one
  visited the other that night (R6). Direction is ignored: A visiting B links them exactly as B visiting A
  would. A group is a set of players linked to each other, directly or through other players. Every player alive at
  the start of the night (including players who die that night) is in exactly one group, so a player who visited no
  one and was visited by no one is a group of 1, and a self-visit links no one. You learn only the sizes, largest
  first (e.g. "4, 2, 1, 1, 1"). This needs no action and a role-block doesn't stop it.
  Night: may also spend a token to map one player (Astral Visit; yourself allowed): at the end of the night you also
  learn the names of everyone in that player's group. A role-block stops the map (R9) but not the sizes.
  Your own actions never visit anyone, so they never link you to anyone.

Scout
  Night: at the end of every night, you learn the names of three players (you may be one of them) who were each in a
  different visit group that night. Groups are as for the Cartographer (visit direction is ignored). The names are
  drawn like this: a random player, then a random player outside the groups already drawn from, and so on, so a big
  group is more likely to come up than a small one. If there were fewer than three groups, you learn one name per
  group and how many groups there were. This needs no action and a role-block doesn't stop it. You never visit
  anyone.

Insomniac
  Tokens: 2 insomniac tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to stay awake. At the end of the night, you learn the roles of up to 3 players who visited
  someone that night (R6; a visit to themselves counts), but not who they are: if more than 3 players visited, 3 of
  them are drawn at random. The roles are listed in alphabetical order, and a role shows twice if two of those
  players have it. If fewer than 3 players visited, you learn all of their roles, and if nobody visited, you learn
  that. Players who visited and then died that night count. Only visits count: an action that isn't a visit (e.g.
  an Astral Visit or a Veteran's alert) doesn't. Staying awake is not a visit. This is an exact-role check (R19).

Accountant
  Night: may audit one player. Learn how many tokens they have in total at the end of the night, after any they
  spent that night and any a Magpie stole (token count, R19). You learn only the total, not what kind of tokens
  they are.

Medic

  Night: may protect one player other than yourself, giving them Standard Defense. Spend 1 token to give Strong
  Defense instead. Spend 1 more token to protect yourself instead (so self-protection with Strong costs 2).

Trapper
  Night: may place a trap on one player other than yourself and other than the player your trap is already on, or
  may remove your trap (removing it isn't a visit). You have one trap at a time; a new trap replaces the old one at

  non-Village player visits the trapped player on a later night, the trap is used up and that visitor is dealt a
  Strong Attack. If several non-Village players visit that night, one of them, chosen at random, is hit. You learn
  that your trap went off, and nothing else (not who, nor whether it killed).

Vigilante
  Tokens: 3 vigilante tokens.
  Night: may shoot one player: 1 token for a Basic Attack, 2 for Standard, 3 for Strong. If your shot kills them,
  you also learn their role (exact-role check, R19).

Veteran
  Tokens: 3 alert tokens.
  You can't be role-blocked.
  Night: may spend a token to go on alert (not a visit, R6, so nothing that reacts to visits counts it). While on
  alert you have Standard Defense and you deal a Strong Attack to every player who visits you that night, whatever
  their faction (a role-blocker who visits you is attacked too), however many there are. Astral Visits aren't
  visits, so they aren't attacked. At the end of the night you learn whether anyone visited you and, if so, how
  many, and whether your attack on each of them succeeded, but nothing about who they were.

Misc

Prosecutor
  Tokens: 2 prosecutor tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to prosecute someone. At the start of the next Day, before anyone speaks, the moderator
  announces that someone is being prosecuted; this counts as a successful nomination and they go to trial. It
  counts toward the Day's three-nomination limit, an execution ends the Day as usual, and it can combine with a
  Clerk's rig. If the trial needs a "nominator", the moderator picks a random player.

Party Animal
  Immune to role-blocks.
  Night: may visit one player, role-blocking them.

Philanthropist
  Tokens: 2 philanthropy tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to hand another player one token of their own role's kind (e.g. a medic token to a
  Medic; one kind chosen at random if their role has several). They are told a Philanthropist handed them a token.
  If their role has no tokens, they are told they threw it away because they have no use for it, so it doesn't
  count toward their tokens (e.g. for the Accountant). You are not told which happened.

Outsiders (Village roles: Good, and win with the Village, but the role helps the Village less or can hurt it)

Roleplayer
  You are told your role is X, chosen at random at the start from Sheriff, Tracker, Lookout, Seer, Fortune Teller,
  Oracle and Accountant.

Ex-Con
  Appears: Evil to alignment checks (R19).
  Night: every night you visit a random player other than yourself, and you aren't told whom. A role-block stops
  the visit (R7).

Cardinal

  victim is drawn from the Good players still alive then, and it counts as a death that night.

All Yakuza share the Katana and night chat (R8).

Grunt
  Night: none of its own.

Pharmacist
  Immune to role-blocks.
  Night: may role-block one player.

Ritualist
  Tokens: 2 ritual tokens.
  Night: may guess one player's exact role (Astral Visit), spending 1 token for a Standard Attack or 2 for a
  Divine Attack. If right, the Attack is dealt. If wrong, the moderator publicly announces at the start of the
  next Day that you are a Ritualist.

Puppeteer
  Tokens: 1 puppet token.
  Night: may spend a token to puppet someone (not yourself or another Yakuza) for the following Day. That Day, they
  are told they are being puppeted, and they can't chat or see private messages; nobody else is told. You chat
  publicly and privately in their place (including seeing their private messages) and can set their claim, which
  appears in the ledger as theirs; that is all you can do for them. They still nominate, vote and so on as normal. It lasts one Day.

Fabricator
  Tokens: 1 fabricator token.
  Night: may visit one non-Yakuza player to frame them (no token needed): that night they appear Evil to
  alignment checks (R19); other results are unchanged. On the same visit, you may spend a token to forge that
  player's last will (not anyone else's): if they die of any cause that night, your forged will replaces theirs.
  Framing and forging together are one visit.

Clerk
  Tokens: 1 clerk token.
  Night: may spend a token to rig the next Day's votes. On a rigged Day, anyone successfully nominated is executed.
  The Guilty/Innocent vote still happens; if a majority votes Guilty, the rig is not announced, otherwise it is
  announced publicly.

Smuggler
  Immune to role-blocks.
  Tokens: 2 swap tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to swap two different living players (yourself included) for the night (R23). You visit
  both of them. Both swapped players are told they were swapped, but not with whom.

Ballot Stuffer
  Tokens: 2 ballot tokens.
  Night: may spend a token so that during the following Day your vote counts twice in every Guilty/Innocent trial
  vote. It does not count twice in nomination (Yes/No) votes, which stay one vote each. A trial that Day needs a
  majority of all votes counted, so your extra vote counts whether you vote Guilty or Innocent. The announced
  totals include your extra vote without saying whose it is.

Fixer
  Tokens: 2 fixer tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to fix one player other than yourself. During the following Day, every Guilty/Innocent
  trial vote they cast counts as the opposite (Guilty as Innocent, Innocent as Guilty). Their nomination (Yes/No)
  votes are unchanged. Nobody is told, not even them: their private reminder shows the vote they cast, while the
  totals and anything that reports how they voted (e.g. the Auditor, the Informant, a Jester's revenge on Guilty
  voters) use the vote as counted.

Diviner
  Night: may pick one player. If they are Yakuza, they get Strong Defense for that night. Otherwise, the group is
  that player plus their nearest neighbor on each side in the circle (R11) among the players alive at the start of
  the night, skipping yourself and never counting anyone twice. You are told who was in the group and the exact
  role of one of them (exact-role check, R19), but not whose it is: it is the player you picked with 60% chance,
  otherwise one of the others (20% each, or 40% if there is only one other). Yakuza in the group and players who

Mortician
  Tokens: 3 mortician tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to try to clean someone. If they die that night by any cause, they are cleaned: their

Wiretap

  You passively see how every player voted in each Guilty/Innocent trial vote, right after the vote. This is not a

Talent Agent

  - Scan: learn one random non-Yakuza role that is in play and one random non-Yakuza role from these rules that

  - Count: name any role in these rules and learn how many players have it in play.

--- Neutral ---
Each Neutral player is their own faction (R2).

Serial Killer
  Defense: Standard. Appears: Not Evil to the Sheriff.
  Win: only alone (not even with another Serial Killer).
  Night: may deal a Strong Attack to one player.

Arsonist
  Defense: Standard. Appears: Not Evil to the Sheriff.
  Win: only alone (not even with another Arsonist).
  Night: may douse one player, or ignite (Astral Visit), dealing a Strong Attack to every doused player. A doused
  player who isn't Good (Yakuza or Neutral) is told at the end of the night that an Arsonist doused them; Good
  players are never told. Igniting uses up every douse: players who survive it are no longer doused.

Jester
  Defense: Basic. Appears: Evil to the Sheriff.
  Never blocks wins (R1).
  Win: iff you are hanged during a Day (other daytime deaths don't count). You lose if the game ends with you
  alive.
  Revenge: if you are hanged, the following night a random Guilty voter from your trial who was alive when that
  night began is dealt a Divine Attack (Astral Visit). If nobody voted Guilty, nothing happens.

Executioner
  Defense: Basic. Appears: Evil to the Sheriff.
  Never blocks wins (R1).
  At the start you get a random target: any player except yourself.
  Win: iff your target is hanged during a Day while you are alive (other daytime deaths don't count). You lose if
  the game ends with your target alive.
  On winning: the moderator reveals you at once and you leave the game. Leaving works exactly like dying (you
  leave the circle for good) except it doesn't count as a death. The following night, a random Guilty voter from
  the trial who was alive when that night began (not you, since you left) is dealt a Divine Attack (Astral Visit). If nobody voted
  Guilty, nothing happens.
  If your target dies any other way, you become a Jester.

Bounty Hunter
  Tokens: 1 attack token. Never blocks wins (R1).
  At the start you get 3 random targets: any players except yourself.
  Night: may spend the token to deal a Strong Attack to one player.
  A bounty on a target is claimed if they die by your attack or are hanged during a Day while your vote counted as
  Guilty. If a target dies any other way (or leaves the game), that bounty is lost. Night deaths are simultaneous
  (R10): a target you kill on the night you die still counts.
  Win: iff you claim 2 bounties. If you are alive then, the moderator reveals you at once and you leave the game
  (leaving works as for the Executioner). If you have died, you still win and nothing is revealed.
  Lose: once you can no longer claim 2 bounties; if you are alive, the moderator reveals you at once and you leave
  the game.

Magpie
  Defense: Basic. Never blocks wins (R1). Random setups include a Magpie only if at least a third of the roles have tokens.
  Night: may steal a token from another player (a visit). It happens at the end of the night, after that night's
  token use, so a token used tonight can't be stolen. The stolen token is gone (you can't use it). You are told

  Win: iff you steal tokens from 3 different players (a second steal from the same player takes nothing). If you
  are alive then, the moderator reveals you at once and you leave the game (as for the Executioner). If you died
  that night, you still win and nothing is revealed.

Vulture
  Win: alone, if you are alive at the start of a Day (after the night's deaths) and max(floor(N/4), 2) or fewer
  players are alive, counting yourself, where N is the number of players at the start of the game. The game then
  ends at once and everyone else loses (wins already earned by roles that never block wins still count, R1).
  Night: none.
  Day: at the start of each Day, you learn a role for each player who died since the previous Day began (during that
  Day or the night after it; not players who left the game): with 50% chance it is their true
  role (exact-role check, R19), otherwise it is a different role drawn at random
  from all the roles in these rules. You aren't told which. This isn't an action, so a role-block doesn't stop it.

Use apply_changes for deaths and token/status changes, tell() for each private result, and end_phase when done. Deaths you apply are announced publicly at dawn automatically, including the kill's cause, so make the cause just the source as the rules allow it to be known (e.g. 'Katana', 'Vigilante', 'Serial Killer', 'Trap'). For each kill also set `by` to the player whose action killed them (the trap's owner for a trap) and katana=true for the Katana attack; these are recorded for analysis, never shown. Don't tell() deaths to all. Every attacked player, including those who died, gets their attack notice (R20 step 5), saying whether they died; moderators have skipped it, or left out the death, for players who died. Tell each role-blocked player that they were role-blocked, even one with no night action or who chose not to act (R9); a role-blocker learns only whether the block failed because its target can't be role-blocked (R9). Write private results in the present, about tonight ('You were role-blocked tonight'), never 'last night': they are delivered at the end of this night. Every player who used an ability gets a private result line, even when nothing else happened (e.g. 'You went on alert. 1 alert token left.'), stating any tokens they have left, except where a role note below says otherwise (e.g. code tells them, so don't tell() them a second result). Tell all Yakuza which actions each Yakuza chose but not the results, nor whether a teammate was role-blocked (R8); role-blocked Yakuza's Katana votes still count. only the attacker learns whether the Katana attack succeeded. Update token counts for any tokens spent. Before end_phase, call record_visits once with every visit that happened tonight (R6, R20 steps 1-2), as [visitor, target] pairs, a self-visit as [X, X] (an empty list if there were none). Easy to miss: the Katana holder visits the Katana target (R8) besides any visit from their own role's action; automatic visits (the Ex-Con's); a Seer's chosen pair is a visit to both players. Leave out the actions of role-blocked players, Astral Visits and actions that target no player. The submitted actions above already show any swap (R23), so record each visit to the player it landed on.

Also handle these roles' effects, using random_choice for anything random:
- A Bloodhound who spent a token (and wasn't role-blocked): use the track op, which spends the token; code tells them the result at the end of the night. Don't tell() the Bloodhound anything about it. It is a visit to the target only. Also, every night while the game has a Bloodhound, use the attacks op once with the attacker of every Attack that happened tonight, fatal or not: the Katana holder for the Katana, a Vigilante's shot, the Serial Killer, a Veteran's alert for each visitor it hits, a Trapper's trap, an Arsonist's ignite, a Ritualist's attack (one entry per attack; repeats allowed; [] if there were none). - A Census Taker who acted (and wasn't role-blocked): use the census op; code draws the group and the count and tells them. Don't tell() the Census Taker anything about it. It is a visit to the target only.
- A Coroner who spent a token (and wasn't role-blocked): use the examine op, which spends the token; code tells them the role and tokens left. Don't tell() the Coroner anything about it. The target must have died before the night began. It is an Astral Visit, not a visit (R6): nothing that reacts to visits sees it.
- A Fixer who spent a token (and wasn't role-blocked): use the fix op, which spends the token; code counts the player's trial votes tomorrow as the opposite; nobody is told. It is a visit to the target only.
- A Philanthropist who spent a token (and wasn't role-blocked): use the give_token op, which spends the token; code hands the recipient a token and tells them. Don't tell() the Philanthropist anything about it.

answers.bugs_or_oddities:
1) Frank's Day 4 public message was just "". It probably reset the Day's no-message round counter (R16) without saying anything.
2) The Yakuza action summaries are worded inconsistently: 'Bob chose no night action' on N2 versus 'Bob chose no Ritualist action' on N1 and N3. Harmless, but uneven.
3) Agent confusion, not engine bugs: on Day 3, Dave wrote 'Bob, Dave wasn't attacked, so my protection proves nothing', which mixes up who is speaking. Bob kept treating his Medic cover as if it were a real action in the Yakuza chat.
4) Everything I checked was consistent with the rules: the setup (2 Yakuza, 0 Neutrals, 5 non-Outsider Village roles including Investigative ones), the census counts (N1: 1 Evil among Carol/Erin/Frank; N2: 1 Evil among Dave/Erin/Frank), the nomination thresholds (4/3/3), the speaking order, the Ritualist's correct guess, and the end-of-game win check after N4 (only Bob and Erin left).
5) A strategic oddity, not a bug: the Village never used the Philanthropist's tokens, which could have refilled Grace's Coroner tokens. And Grace announced her Coroner targets publicly, which made her an obvious Katana target.
answers.suggestions:
1) State plainly whether the Bloodhound learns per-player counts or one combined total, and give a format example.
2) Add a 'submission locked' rule: the last submission before the night closes is final, and chat after it doesn't change it. Show players a confirmation of what they locked in, especially for token spends.
3) Give the moderator a state panel: seat circle, living players, a token ledger, Attack counts per player, a full secret vote log per Day, and active effects (traps, marks, fixes, rigs).
4) Reject empty or whitespace-only public messages, or make them not count as speaking for R16.
5) When the night opens, remind each Yakuza privately of their real role and actions, separate from their public claim, to cut down on cover-versus-role confusion.
6) Consider letting a player who dies at night have results from that same night appended to their will (or explicitly say it can't happen). As it stands, investigators who die the night they act lose their result, which strongly favors the Yakuza in small games.
7) Show the R22 budget numbers in the moderator log.

In this game, the Yakuza's Night 2 proposal cited my census result as the reason to kill me. If you claim an information role, post the result in full immediately, as I did, so the Village keeps it even if you die, and expect the kill. Also consider whether a second, consistent check on the same name next night would give the Village something to cross-check.

lessons.applies_to: Village, especially players who hold a protective role
lessons.tip: Check every claimed Medic's protections against the actual attack map each night. A real Medic protects the likely Katana target, which is usually a publicly claimed information role. Bob's claimed protections went to an unattacked Dave on Nights 2 and 3, while the claimed Census Taker and Coroner were killed unprotected. A pattern of protecting nobody who gets attacked is a strong red flag, and the Village should ask for the protection target directly.

Count the living before you plan a trial. With 4 alive, 3 Yes votes are needed, and with 5 alive, 3 Guilty votes are needed. Two Yakuza can block every nomination. Once the Village is down to a Yakuza pair plus one or two Good players, it can't force a hang without a third vote, so the Village needs confirmed evidence before the head count shrinks.

A Ritualist guess succeeds most often on a player who has claimed Vanilla and has not been challenged, as Dave did. A correct guess removes a Good player for one token, but a wrong guess exposes the Ritualist publicly the next Day. Plan the guess only when the target's claim is already unchallenged, and keep the Fixer for a trial that actually needs flipping.

tips_feedback.tip: Post your role, target and exact result in your first speech after getting it, and counterclaim any copier at once with your full log.
tips_feedback.why: I posted my Night 1 census result on Day 2, and the Yakuza's Night 2 plan explicitly named my census as the reason to kill me. Publishing the result did protect my credibility for the Village, but it made me the first target. The tip doesn't warn about that cost.

tips_feedback.tip: Before voting Guilty, name one concrete mechanical fit: an unexplained Evil read on a Vanilla claim, a broken visit claim, or a group result where elimination leaves one name.
tips_feedback.why: Grace and Dave refused to vote on the census alone or on pressure. Frank's trial then ended Innocent 3-2, and the Village avoided hanging a Good player on a 50/50 read. The same discipline also kept the Village from voting on the census when it had only one Night 1 result.

tips_feedback.tip: Surviving an attack proves nothing. Ask the survivor at once who protected them.
tips_feedback.why: Asking Bob directly about his protection targets (Dave on Night 2, nobody on Night 3) exposed the gap between his Medic claim and the Katana kills of Alice and Grace. The question didn't prove he was Yakuza, but it made his claim visibly unverified before the final votes.

tips_feedback.tip: Never announce tonight's target, in public or by PM.
tips_feedback.why: I kept my Night 2 census target private, and the Yakuza's plan did not rely on it. This tip prevented the target from being disclosed to blockers or the Katana, though the public claim of my Night 1 target on Day 2 was a separate, unhelpful disclosure.

lessons.applies_to: Yakuza with one-shot tokens (Fixer, Ritualist, Clerk, Puppeteer)
lessons.tip: Before spending a one-shot token on a Day effect, check the same night's kill list. My Fixer token went on Dave, who the Ritualist killed that same night, so it did nothing. Spend it on a player who will still be alive to vote, or hold it until you know who survives.

Track the living-count majority math. With 2 Yakuza and 2 Good alive, a nomination needs 3 Yes out of 4, so Good cannot hang anyone and the Yakuza are safe as long as they keep the count at that point. Plan kills so the parity you reach is one Good voters cannot break, rather than killing the last Good voter too early.

lessons.applies_to: Yakuza with a fake protective claim (Medic)
lessons.tip: A fake Medic whose nightly protections never cover the Katana's victims becomes the attack line by Day 3: my Medic protected an unattacked teammate-friendly player while Alice and Grace died unprotected, and three Good players used that gap. Either claim a role with no checkable nightly output, or protect a plausible victim so the claim is consistent with the kill pattern.

A Ritualist guess on a player who keeps publicly claiming an unrevealed role (Dave claimed Vanilla four times) was right and removed a Good voice for one token. Guess when a claim is repeated and unchallenged, and keep the token when the claimant has a live info role that could be checked.

Killing a player who publicly claims an info role can make Good treat that death as proof the role was real, since Good reasons that the Yakuza never kill their own team. Use that: a Katana kill on a claimed Census Taker or Coroner strengthens their claim, so kill info roles only when their results would hurt you before the Day they post.

tips_feedback.tip: Send no daytime PMs about team plans, and none to teammates on Day 2; plan in night chat.
tips_feedback.why: We never sent daytime PMs between Yakuza, so the only team coordination was in night chat and no Good player found a link. The only PMs visible were Frank's and Dave's.

tips_feedback.tip: Every member must submit the agreed Katana holder and target every night; one missing vote can cancel the kill.
tips_feedback.why: Both Yakuza submitted identical holder and target every night, and all four Katana and Ritualist kills landed (Carol, Alice, Grace, Frank) with the Ritualist kill on Dave also succeeding.

tips_feedback.tip: Fake-claim a Village role whose tokens and real visits match yours.
tips_feedback.why: The Medic claim matched my 2 tokens, but the protections it described (Dave on N2, nobody on N3) never covered the Katana victims. Dave, Grace and Frank all used that gap to attack the claim each Day, and the claim never recovered.

tips_feedback.tip: Spend one-shot tokens on the first Day or night they can change a vote or remove a threat.
tips_feedback.why: The Fixer token went on Dave to flip his Day 5 trial vote, but the Ritualist killed Dave the same night, so the token was wasted. The timing idea was right; the target check was not.

tips_feedback.tip: Never claim or name a Yakuza-only role, and never switch claims once cornered.
tips_feedback.why: Bob kept the Medic claim unchanged all game and never named a Yakuza-only role, so no one could catch a switch between Days.

lessons.applies_to: Village information roles (Sheriff, Seer, Coroner, Census Taker, Bloodhound, Tracker, Lookout)
lessons.tip: The Yakuza kill whoever threatens them, so a claimed information role that is Katana-killed the night after posting or examining is probably genuine. Cross-check every protector claim against the kill list: a Medic who protects an unattacked player on the nights when claimed info roles die is the strongest Yakuza tell this game.

Do not wait for a perfect read. Here the Village waited from Day 2 to Day 4 for a Coroner result, and with 4-5 alive a trial needs 3 Yes, so the Yakuza removed one Village player per night while nominations failed 1 Yes and 2 Yes three times. Agree on a deadline and a threshold early, and vote on the best available read by Day 3 even if it is imperfect.

Post each night's target, role and exact result publicly in your first speech after it happens, and do it before anyone else can make the claim their own. Carol's Bloodhound result and Alice's census were held or contested, and the Village argued over whether Alice was a real Census Taker for days. A night result announced early is hard to call a single unverified claim.

The Bloodhound's attack count is cumulative, so track it. Record each of the three names' counts every night; a player whose count rises after a Katana kill is the holder. Pre-write your planned target and any results in the will, since a result that arrives on the night you die is only reachable through the will.

A fake protector claim survives only while nobody checks its target against the kills. Keep the Medic claim's targets plausible (protect the claimed info role on nights they are likely to be hit), and never let a clearly unattacked target be the only one protected while info roles die unprotected.

tips_feedback.tip: Before voting Guilty, name one concrete mechanical fit (a single Evil read or broken claim).
tips_feedback.why: Village followed it so strictly that nobody could be hanged on the census alone. Nominations failed on 1 Yes and 2 Yes three times, while the Yakuza killed a Village player every night. The principle is sound, but the Village needed a lower bar for a trial by Day 3.

tips_feedback.tip: Fake-claim a Village role whose tokens and real visits match yours; Medic claims with protection on likely Katana targets.
tips_feedback.why: Bob (Ritualist) claimed Medic with 2 tokens, which matched the Ritualist's token count. The Village never demanded his protection targets until Day 3, so the false claim survived four Days. Helped the Yakuza, hurt the Village.

tips_feedback.tip: Coroner: examine bodies that settle live questions, and post the night, target and role in one message.
tips_feedback.why: Grace's Night 2 Carol result (Bloodhound, Village) was posted and cleared a suspect. But Grace died on Night 3 after examining Alice, so the Alice read never reached the Village, which was the one result that mattered most.

lessons.tip: Every private message shows publicly as sender-to-recipient (R4), so a private nomination pact is visible the moment it is sent. Frank's PMs to Dave ('let's nominate Erin together') were public. Coordinate in public or not at all.

lessons.applies_to: Village info roles (Census Taker, Coroner, Sheriff, Seer and similar)
lessons.tip: The Yakuza killed each publicly claimed info role within one night of its first result (Alice on N2, Grace on N3). Post every result the next morning in the same message as your claim, not on a later scheduled Day. Grace held her Alice result until a planned Day 4 post and died with it, so the Village never got that check.

A trial needs a majority of living players, and the Yakuza only need to survive each Day. With 5 alive, Village had 3 Good votes on Day 3 but split on Frank, and the 2-2 Day 4 nominations then failed. Two-versus-two is a Yakuza win. Don't wait for a read that the Yakuza can kill first. Nominate the strongest mechanical contradiction while the majority still exists.

Check each Medic claim against the attack list every night. A real Medic protects the publicly claimed info role that is likely to be hit. Bob's Medic 'protected' Dave on N2 when nobody was attacked, and protected nobody on the nights Alice and Grace died. Matching token counts (2 Medic tokens, same as a Ritualist's) proves nothing.

A Ritualist guess of Vanilla Villager is the cheapest Standard kill, because Vanilla has Defense None and most Village are Vanilla. Don't spend a Fixer token on a target the same night a Katana or Ritualist hit lands on them: Erin's Fixer on Dave was wasted when Dave died that night.

tips_feedback.tip: Before voting Guilty, name one concrete mechanical fit (...). A role-block fully explains a missing result.
tips_feedback.why: I followed it strictly, and with no mechanical proof on Day 2 or Day 4 nobody nominated. The stall favored the Yakuza, who killed one player every night (Carol N1, Alice N2, Grace N3, Dave and Frank N4) while Village waited for a read.

tips_feedback.tip: Each night write your planned target in your will, and post results publicly by day. The result of the night you die never reaches your will.
tips_feedback.why: Accurate and useful as a warning. Grace's Night 2 Carol result came out on Day 3 and was trusted, but her Night 3 Alice result died with her, which is exactly the failure this tip predicts. Posting the same morning would have helped.

tips_feedback.tip: Fake-claim a Village role whose tokens and real visits match yours (Yakuza tip).
tips_feedback.why: Bob's Medic claim with 2 tokens (matching a Ritualist's) went unchallenged for most of the game. The protection gap was only raised on Day 4, after the Village had lost tempo.

tips_feedback.tip: Answer a direct question about your night action in one plain sentence the first time it is asked.
tips_feedback.why: Erin's plain 'Vanilla Villager' answer came only after a visible wobble ('no night action' first), but once stated it was never broken and made Erin look settled.

lessons.applies_to: Yakuza with a Fixer, Clerk, Puppeteer or other one-shot token
lessons.tip: Before spending a one-shot token, check whether a teammate's kill or block this same night already removes the target. On Night 4 I spent my Fixer token on Dave while Bob's Ritualist guess also targeted Dave. The flip was wasted because Dave died that night. Agree in night chat which of you spends which token, and drop any token whose only use depends on the target surviving.

lessons.applies_to: Yakuza posing as a protective claim (Medic, or any claim with night protections)
lessons.tip: A fake Medic is structurally exposed. The Yakuza choose the Katana victim, so the Village can compare who was protected with who died. Bob's claim protected an unattacked player on Nights 2 and 3 while the claimed info roles died unprotected. Choose protection targets that are plausible Katana victims, or prefer a claim with no checkable night outcomes, such as Vanilla.

lessons.applies_to: Yakuza posing as a Village role
lessons.tip: Give one role wording from the first speech and repeat it exactly. My early 'no night action' phrasing, later changed to 'Vanilla Villager', gave Frank a line of attack for three Days. A simple claim with no night action is safe only if it is stated identically every time.

Count the nomination threshold before a Day. At 4 alive, 3 Yes votes are needed, so a 2-2 split with a Yakuza on each side stops every trial. Keep the Village split on a census claim that cannot be checked, and do not push a trial that needs a Village vote you cannot get.
Submit the agreed holder and target every night and keep daytime plans out of private messages. This worked perfectly: no mismatched submissions, and no daytime PMs about team plans.

tips_feedback.tip: Every member must submit the agreed Katana holder and target every night; one missing vote can cancel the kill.
tips_feedback.why: Bob and I submitted matching holder and target on all four nights, so all four Katana attacks landed (Carol, Alice, Grace, Frank).

tips_feedback.tip: Send no daytime PMs about team plans, and none to teammates on Day 2; plan in night chat.
tips_feedback.why: All our team planning stayed in the night chat, so the Village could not see our coordination during the day. Only Frank's and Dave's private messages were visible.

tips_feedback.tip: Fake-claim a Village role whose tokens and real visits match yours. Never claim or name a Yakuza-only role.
tips_feedback.why: A fake Medic's protections cannot match real outcomes, because the Yakuza pick the victim. Bob's Medic claim protected an unattacked player while the claimed info roles died unprotected. The Village saw the gap and pushed on it for days, so the tip hurt more than it helped.

tips_feedback.tip: Never switch claims once cornered.
tips_feedback.why: My first wording, 'no night action', was then changed to 'Vanilla Villager' under questioning. Frank used that wobble as his main line of attack for three Days, which cost us tempo and gave the Village a reason to keep Erin in play.

tips_feedback.tip: Tokens die with you. Spend one-shot tokens on the first Day or night they can change a vote or remove a threat.
tips_feedback.why: I spent my Fixer token on Dave on Night 4, but Bob's Ritualist guess killed Dave the same night. The token did nothing. The tip is sound in general, but it must be checked against what a teammate is already doing that night.

lessons.applies_to: Village, especially players without a night role
lessons.tip: Judge each claimed Medic by whether their protections line up with actual Katana attacks. A Medic who protects an unattacked player while a publicly claimed info role dies unprotected, night after night, is the strongest tell available. Check this before weighing any other read.

Do not wait for a perfect read when you already have a credible one. The Yakuza kill one claimed info role per night, so every Day of waiting for a Coroner or Census Taker result to be posted costs you a source. Nominate once the evidence points one way, and say in advance what result would change your vote.

A Ritualist guess on a player who has openly claimed Vanilla Villager is a cheap, high-value kill. If it is wrong, you only lose one token and a cover. If it is right, the Village loses a player and has no way to check the attack. Use it when the Village has no reliable way to verify the target.

A Vanilla Villager claim that the Village can't disprove is a strong cover. Erin's unchallenged Vanilla claim survived all game while the Village argued about it, so pick a Village role whose claim has no checkable result.

Repeated accusations and 'I'm not nominating' loops spend budget without adding information. Each public message should add one new mechanical fact or one concrete question. My budget fell to about 1 by Day 4 from repeating the same census argument.

tips_feedback.tip: Before voting Guilty, name one concrete mechanical fit (a Vanilla claim with an unexplained Evil read, a broken visit claim, or a group result).
tips_feedback.why: Village used this as a reason to wait, and no concrete fit ever appeared. Meanwhile the Yakuza killed Alice and Grace, so the requirement became a stall that favored them.

tips_feedback.tip: Medic: use free Standard protection on likely Katana targets, and never announce targets.
tips_feedback.why: It gave a clear standard to measure Bob's claimed protections against. Bob protected an unattacked player on Night 2 and nobody on Night 3 while claimed info roles died, which exposed the gap.

tips_feedback.tip: Fake-claim a Village role whose tokens and real visits match yours. Never claim a Yakuza-only role.
tips_feedback.why: Erin's Vanilla Villager claim was never mechanically disproven, and it helped the Yakuza survive the trials and win. Village had no tool to test it.

tips_feedback.tip: Surviving an attack proves nothing, since Arsonists and Serial Killers have Standard Defense.
tips_feedback.why: Not wrong as a rule, but irrelevant to this game because no Neutral killer was present. It did not affect any decision.

lessons.applies_to: Coroner, Census Taker, and any claimed information role
lessons.tip: Post results the moment they arrive and never pre-announce tonight's examination target. I wrote 'tonight I examine Alice' on Day 3, and the Yakuza's night plan explicitly cited my Alice read as the threat before killing me. A public claim already makes you a Katana target, so the announcement adds nothing but a clearer kill order.

Check every Medic claim against the attack record each night. Bob's claimed protections went to Dave twice, and Dave was never attacked, while the publicly claimed information roles Alice and Grace died unprotected. A real Medic covers a claimed info role when the Katana is likely to hit one, so a Medic who protects only unattacked players is a strong lead. Make them name the target publicly the day after and compare it to who died.

Do not stall for three Days waiting on one read. Every night without a trial is a free Katana kill for the Yakuza, and the Village lost Carol, Alice, Grace, Dave and Frank this way. Even with partial information, get one nomination and trial through each Day, and aim it at the claim with the worst mechanical gap, not at the loudest accuser.

Once the living count reaches 4 with 2 Yakuza, a 2-2 split can never produce a majority, so the Yakuza win by simply surviving and killing one Village player per night. Village must force a hang while the count is still odd or with a Yakuza-vs-Village majority available; waiting for 3 Yes at 4 alive is a losing plan.

A public Vanilla claim is a free Ritualist guess. Dave's 'Vanilla Villager' post let Bob spend one token for a correct Standard kill, and nobody on Village had a Medic who covered him. Also, a Medic claim with protections on unattacked players survived three Days because nobody demanded the target in the moment, and a 'no night action' wobble followed by a clean Vanilla claim cost Erin nothing.

tips_feedback.tip: Never announce tonight's target, in public or by PM.
tips_feedback.why: The tip was accurate: my public Day 3 'I examine Alice tonight' post was used by the Yakuza as the reason to kill me. I broke the spirit of this tip, and that cost me directly.

tips_feedback.tip: On Day 2, power roles with no result should not hint at their role or lead loudly. The most organized voice is the usual Night 2 kill.
tips_feedback.why: Alice led loudly with a public Census Taker claim on Day 2 and was Katana-killed on Night 2, as predicted. The tip is a reliable warning about who the Yakuza target first.

tips_feedback.tip: Before voting Guilty, name one concrete mechanical fit (an unexplained Evil read, a broken visit claim, or a group result).
tips_feedback.why: I followed it strictly and held Innocent on Frank and refused any nomination until Alice's read. That kept Village from trading any execution for three Days, while the Yakuza killed a Village player every night. The tip is sound for a single vote, but as a blanket rule it produced a stall that the Yakuza could exploit.

tips_feedback.tip: Fake-claim a Village role whose tokens and real visits match yours. Never switch claims once cornered.
tips_feedback.why: This was the Yakuza side's playbook. Bob's Medic claim (with tokens and nightly protection stories) was never checked against attacks, and Erin's 'no night action' wobble was smoothed into 'Vanilla' without a penalty. It helped the Yakuza win.

tips_feedback.tip: Coroner: examine bodies that settle live questions; post the night, target and role in one message the next Day.
tips_feedback.why: My Night 2 Carol read was posted publicly on Day 3 and cleared Carol, which narrowed the census to Erin or Frank. The tip was right about posting the result the next Day; my error was the pre-announcement.

summary: The Yakuza (Bob, Ritualist, and Erin, Fixer) won a 7-player game with only two members. The Katana never missed: it killed the Bloodhound (Carol) on N1, the Census Taker (Alice) on N2 and the Coroner (Grace) on N3, and nobody was protected. The Village had a strong lead from the start. Alice's N1 census found exactly 1 Evil among Carol, Erin and Frank. Carol was a Katana victim, so the Evil was Erin or Frank. Erin also dodged her role claim twice on Day 2. Still, the Village made no nomination on Day 2 with 6 alive. On Day 3, with 5 alive, Dave and Grace voted No on Frank's nomination of Erin. They wanted to wait for Grace's Day 4 Coroner read of Alice. That read added almost nothing: Alice was a Katana victim, and Census Taker isn't one of the roles a Roleplayer can be told. Waiting also gave the game away. Grace had publicly promised the result, so the Yakuza killed her on N3. That left 2v2, where two Yakuza can block every nomination (3 Yes needed of 4). On Day 4 every nomination failed 2-2. On N4 Bob made a Ritualist guess that Dave was a Vanilla Villager, which Dave had claimed publicly, while the Katana killed Frank. The double kill ended the game. Yakuza mistakes went unpunished. Erin's claim wobble, Bob's Medic claim (he never protected the claimed info roles) and Bob's votes with Erin were all spotted, but the Village never acted on them. Erin also held her Fixer token through Frank's 2-3 Day 3 trial, where fixing one Innocent voter would have hanged him.

lessons.tip: Count down to the point where you can't win any more. If the Yakuza can block every nomination after one more night kill (e.g. 2 Yakuza at 4 alive, where 3 Yes are needed), the Day before that is your last chance. Hang your best suspect then, even on a 50/50, and don't wait for a result that only arrives after the next night.
lessons.evidence: On Day 3, with 5 alive, Frank's nomination of Erin got only 1 Yes. Dave and Grace held out for Grace's Day 4 read. Grace died on N3, and on Day 4 every nomination failed 2-2. With Frank, Dave and Grace voting Guilty, a trial on Erin would have hanged her 3-2.

lessons.tip: Treat a Katana victim as near-certainly non-Yakuza, and remember that a Roleplayer is only ever told one of Sheriff, Tracker, Lookout, Seer, Fortune Teller, Oracle or Accountant. A dead Census Taker or Coroner who was Katana-killed doesn't need confirming. Act on their result at once.
lessons.evidence: Grace spent both Coroner tokens on Katana victims (Carol, then Alice). The Village delayed a whole Day to 'verify' Alice's census, even though Alice couldn't have been a Roleplayer and had been killed by the Katana.

lessons.tip: Don't publicly promise that tomorrow's result will decide the game. It tells the Yakuza exactly whom to kill tonight. If a result truly matters, say who you're examining in your will, not in chat, and push for the vote today.
lessons.evidence: Grace said repeatedly that her Day 4 read of Alice would settle the census. The Yakuza night chat picked Grace on N3 specifically to remove that check.

lessons.tip: Save Ritualist tokens until a public claim makes the guess nearly certain, especially a Vanilla Villager claim. An endgame guess combined with the Katana gives a two-kill night that can end the game at once.
lessons.evidence: Bob held both tokens until N4, then guessed that Dave, who had openly claimed Vanilla, was a Vanilla Villager. Together with the Katana kill on Frank, that killed both remaining Villagers and won the game.

lessons.tip: Fix a likely Innocent voter the night before the first Day with a contested trial. One flipped vote decides a close trial, and a token held back may never matter.
lessons.evidence: Erin used no Fixer token before Day 3. Frank's trial failed 2 Guilty to 3 Innocent, so fixing Dave or Grace would have hanged a Villager. The token she finally spent on N4 was wasted because Dave died that night.

lessons.tip: Have a full role claim ready before Day 2 and give it in your first message. A vague 'no night action' invites several rounds of pressure, and other players start citing it as evidence.
lessons.evidence: Erin opened with 'no night action' and only said 'Vanilla Villager' after Dave, Alice, Frank and Grace pressed her. Frank built his whole case on that wobble, and only the Village's caution saved her.

lessons.tip: When one suspect is narrowed to two names, look at who keeps shielding the more likely one and voting with them. A fake protector claim whose 'protections' never cover the claimed info roles is a strong second-Yakuza lead.
lessons.evidence: Bob claimed Medic, but he protected the never-attacked Dave on N2 and nobody on N3, while Alice and Grace died. He said 'let's not pile on Erin' and was the only player besides Erin to vote Guilty on Frank. Dave noticed all of this but never turned it into a vote.

tips_feedback.tip: Before voting Guilty, name one concrete mechanical fit: an unexplained Evil read on a Vanilla claim, a broken visit claim, or a group result where elimination leaves one name.
tips_feedback.why: Dave and Grace used it to refuse a 50/50 census hang on the last Day the Village could still hang anyone. They waited for a 'mechanical' result that never came, then lost to the 2v2 lock.

tips_feedback.tip: Never announce tonight's target, in public or by PM. A Wiretap may read every PM, and a named target tells blockers and the Katana where to go.
tips_feedback.why: Grace ignored it and kept saying she would examine Alice and that the result would decide the census. The Yakuza killed her on N3 for exactly that reason, which shows the tip was right.

tips_feedback.tip: Answer a direct question about your night action in one plain sentence the first time it is asked; days of evasion become a case of their own.
tips_feedback.why: Erin's 'no night action' before 'Vanilla' became Frank's main case against her and nearly got her nominated. That supports the tip.

tips_feedback.tip: Every member must submit the agreed Katana holder and target every night; one missing vote can cancel the kill.
tips_feedback.why: Bob and Erin confirmed identical holder and target votes in night chat every night, and all four Katana kills landed.

tips_feedback.tip: Send no daytime PMs about team plans, and none to teammates on Day 2; plan in night chat.
tips_feedback.why: The Yakuza never PM'd each other by day, so no link showed. Frank's daytime PMs to Dave were turned against him when Erin cited them as pressure.

tips_feedback.tip: Tokens die with you. Spend one-shot tokens on the first Day or night they can change a vote or remove a threat.
tips_feedback.why: Bob's well-timed Ritualist token won the game. Erin's held Fixer token is the counterexample: used before Day 3, it would have hanged Frank, and it was wasted on N4.

tips_feedback.tip: Examine bodies that settle live questions: one side of a duplicate claim, or a hanged suspect.
tips_feedback.why: Grace examined only Katana victims, whose alignment was already near-certain, so her tokens settled nothing live. Following the tip would have pointed her toward pushing for a hang instead.

issues.description: On Night 1, Bob reported that the night-chat prompt tells players to fill only the message and ready fields, even though the Katana holder and target fields are needed for the Yakuza vote. The prompt should say clearly whether the Katana fields should be left empty or filled in during chat turns, so the Yakuza don't miss or garble their vote.

Late on Day 4, Frank posted a public message that was just an empty string (`Frank (public): ""`). The harness accepted it, probably spent his budget on it, and counted it as public activity for the Day-length rule. Empty messages should be rejected or treated as a pass.

In the post-game debrief, both Frank and Dave failed with 'empty answer (error_max_structured_output_retries, stop_reason tool_use)'. The structured-output step for dead players' debrief answers broke, so their feedback was lost.

The Bloodhound text says you learn the three names 'and how many Attacks they have made in total'. It doesn't say whether that is one total per player or one combined total for the group. The program gave a single combined number ('together they have made 1 attack'). The rule text should say which one is meant.

Several Village players (Frank on Days 3–4, Dave on Day 4) treated 'Yakuza never kill their own team, so Katana victims are Good' as a mechanical certainty. Frank called it 'mechanical proof'. No rule stops the Yakuza from attacking a teammate, so this is a strong inference, not a guarantee.

On Day 2, Dave said 'A Philanthropist can't verify his own alignment'. Every player knows their own role and alignment. The fair point is only that others can't verify Frank's claim. Several players echoed the same idea.

In the Night 2 Yakuza chat, Bob (the real Ritualist, publicly claiming Medic) said 'My Medic action goes on Grace', as if his fake claim were real. Erin had to remind him that he has no protection action.
